Pulsar references: Java baseline decision, topics and resource management, retention versus TTL, broker configuration API. Server storage identity and recovery must be validated for the chosen deployment. Envelope and consumer rules Version 1 includes pipeline/subscriptionId/generation/event ID, kind/namespace, table/schema version, source position and sequence. Publication IDs include subscription identity to prevent deduplication across different mappings; Change.eventId still identifies the logical source event. Values are interpreted through the schema. Numeric strings retain precision; present: false means absent and present: true, value: null means SQL NULL. JSON null is a JSON text value and differs from SQL NULL. Kind Meaning --- --- SCHEMA Columns/types/identity/source indexes; message sinks do not execute DDL/index conversion SNAPSHOT BEGIN , SNAPSHOT ROW , SNAPSHOT END Snapshot ID/baseline/parts/row ordinals/counts; complete only after END and deduplicated counts match BEGIN , ROW , COMMIT Source commit boundary/order/before/after images; COMMIT is published after all row confirmations Primary-key updates expose both beforeKey and afterKey : remove the old identity and insert/update the new identity. Keyless duplicate rows each have a separate rowId. Delete the specified occurrence, not all equal rows. Snapshot and CDC share these occurrence identities. Transaction controls include global totalChanges , per-namespace expectedChanges , transactionKind and source attributes; controls preserve BARRIER changes at their original ordinals. Row ordinals cover the whole transaction projected to that destination. Consumers should durably stage and deduplicate events, await the required rows and COMMIT, verify counts/order, then atomically commit their business work and consumer checkpoint. Different queues/subjects can be consumed at different speeds: an application may observe COMMIT before all rows arrive. COMMIT contentHash is the Codec SHA-256 of the normalized SourceTransaction projected through this destination's mappings. A consumer subscribed to every mapped namespace can reconstruct it from BEGIN's transaction ID/generation/position/kind/attributes and ordered ROW.change values. A consumer of only some namespaces cannot claim to verify the entire hash. Transport epochs are headers outside immutable bodies. Track generation/sequence to prevent late old publications from overwriting newer state; timestamps are not source order. Neither the NATS duplicate window nor Rabbit message IDs replace durable consumer deduplication. Consumer ACKs, crashes, transaction staging capacity, missing rows and long outages require a consumer recovery protocol; this version does not ship an automatically running materialization consumer. Kafka producer idempotence also does not cover all replay after replacing a producer instance. Broker offsets are not source sequences. Handle late old-owner publications through generation/epoch/logical sequence/event ID, not physical offset alone. Consumers selecting one namespace filter envelopes and verify that namespace's expectedChanges. Recovery and FAQ Disconnect/restart: retryable failures preserve checkpoints, reconnect, revalidate established resources and replay unconfirmed work. Permanent permission/routing/property failures pause only that destination. Repair and select its generation-bound Resume action in the UI. Missing queue/stream: MESSAGE DESTINATION MISSING REBUILD REQUIRED requires restoring original broker storage or a recovery plan covering consumers, missing history and a new snapshot. Creating an empty resource and pressing Resume cannot prove historical completeness. An administrator purging/replacing a same-name resource or changing broker policies cannot be detected by an existence check alone; reconcile the data. Cross-target atomicity: destinations confirm independently. One may succeed while another fails. There is no cross-database/broker distributed transaction. Source history remains until lagging subscribers catch up; quota exhaustion stops capture rather than dropping their data. Pause/cutover: message destinations return UNCONFIRMED IN FLIGHT PUBLICATION . A journal epoch cannot retract a broker request already in flight. Fence/stop old producers, establish downstream catch-up barriers, reconcile and isolate business writes before cutover. Automated cutover remains in development. Oversized messages: MESSAGE TOO LARGE preserves the transaction checkpoint. Align application/broker limits and consumer memory. Transparent fragmentation/external LOB storage is unimplemented. Large source transactions, catalog memory and growing receipt history still require resource work; there is no hardware-independent capacity guarantee. Redis confirmation does not arrive: inspect AOF health, required replica AOF fsyncs, replication lag, disk and ACL. REDIS DURABILITY NOT CONFIRMED or REDIS CONNECTION CHANGED DURING CONFIRM leaves publication unconfirmed and replayable, even if XADD already reached the server. Fix the cause without deleting stream history or weakening a running task's durability configuration. The UI's source snapshot rows are source preparation progress; per-destination snapshot confirmations are separate and still do not prove consumer completion. Verification: run SYNC MAVEN CACHE=/path/to/cache bash tests/messaging-run.sh . It creates/restarts/removes only its own Compose project. See validation for versions, results and remaining cluster/TLS acceptance. Protocol references: Kafka 3.9 Java baseline, producer configuration, Rabbit Java client/Java 8 baseline, Rabbit reliability, NATS Java client, JetStream. Protocol documentation does not substitute for this project's environment acceptance. Redis references: WAITAOF same-connection semantics and returned counts, persistence, Jedis. The current client is Jedis 8.0.2 using its single-connection API. RocketMQ native TCP profile The ROCKETMQ publisher is implemented using Java-8-compatible native client 5.5.1 with isolated dependencies. Real native-broker confirmation, client/broker restart, unsafe flush refusal and lost-topic protection passed ( target/rocketmq-transport-cached.log ); mixed snapshot/CDC, worker kill and three broker restart rounds passed ( target/messaging-rocketmq-mixed.log , 49 executions). Cluster, ACL and TLS support are not claimed. The first profile is a single ASYNC MASTER broker group with one local synchronous disk copy , not a synchronous replicated or Raft guarantee. replicas must be 1; username/password/token are rejected until an authenticated profile is verified. Use a trusted network for this profile. Configure rocketmq://nameserver:9876 , optional additional NameServers in messaging.endpoints , cluster , broker , topic and minimumRetentionHours . The URI is a native TCP NameServer, not a 5.x gRPC Proxy. topic is a prefix of 1–48 characters (letter first, then letters/digits/underscore/hyphen). The physical topic is prefix 64-hex task/subscription/generation binding . The UI exposes that actual name once the journal generation exists. New generations receive different names; restarting the same generation reuses its name. Reserve these names exclusively for Rivomesh and prohibit external creation, deletion, expansion or writes. Preparation reads broker configuration and creates exactly one read/write queue on the selected broker group. The broker must have flushDiskType=SYNC FLUSH , transientStorePoolEnable=false , autoCreateTopicEnable=false , cleanFileForciblyEnable=false , and fileReservedTime = minimumRetentionHours (default 87600 hours). DLedger/controller/replicated profiles are rejected. Deploy these durability settings at broker startup; do not change storage mode live. The client sends persistent synchronous messages with waitStoreMsgOK and accepts only SEND OK ; disk/slave timeout statuses do not advance the journal checkpoint. Retries can duplicate events with the same stable ID. Queue offset 0 contains an ownership manifest identified by user property rivomesh publication manifest . Consumers must filter this manifest before decoding JSON envelopes. Subsequent messages use the common event envelope and rivomesh event id , rivomesh channel , rivomesh key properties. All logical tables/control channels share queue 0. Consumers still deduplicate and verify SNAPSHOT END / COMMIT and row counts; native broker confirmation does not mean application completion. The manifest permits a crash between topic creation and publication to finish on restart. A nonempty topic with another manifest, missing initialized topic, changed queue/policy, or expired offset 0 blocks with a recovery error. Each publication batch rechecks broker settings, topic shape and manifest. No automatic empty-history replacement is permitted. Retention is finite : plan downstream archival and a verified rebuild before its horizon; large retention values are not infinite storage. Storage loss, manual cleanup, quota and retention expiry require a recovery plan. Monitor broker disk capacity; do not lower retention to clear pressure silently. Run bash tests/rocketmq-transport-run.sh for the actual release-JAR/broker test. The test uses isolated native broker 5.5.0, no host ports, startup data-volume ownership initialization and removes only its Compose project. The default anonymous single-node test does not validate ACL, TLS, power loss, controller/DLedger, replica failover or sustained throughput. Protocol references: server configuration and native client source. A matching manifest alone does not prove retained confirmed history. RocketMQ now also persists and verifies a native confirmation receipt as described below. Other message transports still need their own rollback-detection profiles; do not infer that this protects every broker product. RocketMQ native confirmation receipts After a successful publication batch, the journal saves a generation-bound native receipt before schema/snapshot/transaction receipts advance. New table publication transport contains one small row per subscription; this additive table is created when opening existing journals. Its update is lease-fenced and compares the previously read receipt, so a stale worker cannot replace a newer receipt. Confirmation loss or an uncertain metadata commit still replays stable IDs. ROCKETMQ OFFSET V1 binds the physical topic, queue offset, CommitLog byte offset and a SHA-256 digest of the stable event ID plus message body. On reconnect and before each publication batch, native viewMessage reads the CommitLog record and verifies that receipt. This avoids treating asynchronous ConsumeQueue indexing lag as lost confirmed data. Missing, replaced or changed confirmed records block that destination with ROCKETMQ CONFIRMED HISTORY REBUILD REQUIRED , before further publication or resource creation. Normal restart resumes against the saved receipt. An existing publication without its required native receipt blocks with PUBLICATION TRANSPORT UPGRADE REQUIRES PLAN ; a new binary does not invent an unsafe baseline for an older task. target/rocketmq-native-progress-restore.log passed the actual release-JAR test: stop broker, copy its nonempty volume after the first confirmation, restart and confirm another event, restore the older volume, verify the first event remains while the second is missing, and reject continuation with the saved later receipt. It also rejects a changed content digest and accepts a matching receipt through client restart. target/messaging-native-progress.log additionally passed 53 executions: the actual release JAR, six message products plus PostgreSQL, worker kill and three all-broker stop/start rounds with native receipt recovery. These checks protect the saved confirmed record; they are not an arbitrary-history checksum or consumer business checkpoint. Keep the ownership/retention/storage requirements, consumer count/order verification and archival plan. Do not delete the transport receipt or force a lower offset to bypass failure. A validated recovery/rebuild plan is required when confirmed history has been lost. Receipt rows and other metadata require physical storage headroom beyond the logical event quota. target/v3-native-progress-external.log passed 47 executions, including the native receipt persistence/CAS/lease/reopen contract against actual MySQL, PostgreSQL and openGauss journal storage, plus V3 SQL fan-out and HTTP controls. target/ui-native-progress.log passed 16 DOM tests. Artemis Core retained-queue profile ACTIVEMQ ARTEMIS is a separate product from ActiveMQ Classic. Configure artemis://host:61616 , username/password, explicit database mappings and messaging.stream as a 1–48-character queue prefix (letter first, then letters/digits/underscore/hyphen). messaging.broker optionally checks the broker name. The first profile accepts one entrance, replicas: 1 and no token/extra endpoints. The physical queue is prefix . 64-hex pipeline/subscription/generation binding ; the UI exposes it after generation initialization. The client speaks Core protocol through isolated rivomesh-artemis-transport . Java 8 compatibility uses Core client 2.19.1 with privately pinned Netty 4.1.130 and separate logging/JSON libraries. Current clients requiring Java 11 are not loaded into a Java 8 worker. Acceptance is against broker 2.57.0, whose runtime is independent of the worker JDK. This is a tested compatibility profile, not a claim that every older client/broker/security configuration is supported. The broker must enable persistence, transactional and nontransactional journal sync; preparation reads these runtime attributes. Keep journal-datasync=true in the broker configuration: the management attributes used here do not independently expose/verify that setting. The supplied broker fixture sets it explicitly and uses NIO. Physical storage durability and power-loss acceptance remain separate requirements. A synchronous Core transaction commit precedes publication receipts; lost confirmations still permit stable-ID duplicates. Use a dedicated address-settings match such as rivomesh. for that prefix. Disable auto-create queues/addresses and all auto-delete variants for business resources; the service explicitly creates its first reserved queue. Disable expiry ( no-expiry=true , or all expiry delays -1), last-value/ring/purge behavior and delivery discard ( max-delivery-attempts=-1 ). PAGE/BLOCK/FAIL address policies are accepted; DROP is rejected. A persistent non-destructive ANYCAST queue with exactly one queue bound to its address is required. Existing incompatible resources are refused. Do not change journal-datasync or these policies underneath a running task. Management travels over the same authenticated Core connection, not a separate HTTP admin URL. It uses a temporary non-durable activemq.management. uuid reply queue. Grant the needed management, temporary-queue create/delete, send/consume/browse rights and allow cleanup for this internal prefix. Check creates no business objects; its temporary control channel closes afterward. Do not apply the business no-create policy to this reply prefix. The example fixture separates these address settings; merge the relevant settings into an existing deployment rather than replacing its entire broker configuration blindly. Queue offset/record ordering is internal to Artemis. A retained ownership message carries rivomesh publication manifest ; consumers filter that property before decoding subsequent bytes as the common JSON envelope. Published properties carry rivomesh event id , rivomesh channel , rivomesh key and the common headers. Normal consumer ACK does not delete messages from this non-destructive queue. After reconnect consumers may receive older events again and must use durable deduplication/business checkpoints. Native Core byte consumption is tested; AMQP/JMS consumer variants still need their own interoperability acceptance. The service binds the broker's persistent node ID and queue ID in the journal after preparation. Missing initialized queues, changed incarnations, wrong ownership or unsafe queue shape block before publication receipts advance. Preparation can finish an interrupted empty reserved queue; initialized resources are not replaced. The identity is rechecked around publication. After each confirmed batch, the journal also saves ARTEMIS RECORD V1 with physical queue, native message ID, event ID and a length-prefixed event/body SHA-256. Before resuming or sending another batch, a filtered Core browser checks that exact persistent record and content. Missing/changed history blocks even when a restored older nonempty backup retains the same node/queue IDs. This checks the last saved confirmation, not every earlier record or downstream business checkpoint. Existing publications without a native receipt require an explicit migration/rebuild plan; never clear metadata to continue. An empty initialized replacement is rejected without writing a new ownership message. Why does ACK retain history? This profile intentionally keeps the publication log. Plan disk capacity, consumer archival and an explicit rebuild/retention workflow; normal consumer ACK does not reclaim this queue. Can I use an ordinary destructive queue? No; it fails profile validation. Can I point this at ActiveMQ Classic? No; Classic has a distinct protocol/profile and is not implemented by this adapter. Why did Check fail with permissions? In addition to data access, Core management needs its temporary reply-channel grants. The response does not expose credentials or message contents. target/artemis-transport-volume-fixed.log passed Java 8 client/current-broker publication, exact bytes/key/channel, non-destructive consumer ACK, broker/client restart with stable identities, unsafe queue refusal and missing initialized queue protection. Its first failed log concerned isolated data-volume permissions, not protocol acceptance. target/artemis-wiring-unit.log passed 44 core executions; target/ui-artemis-fixed.log passed 17 DOM cases after fixing a product-switch credential visibility bug. Earlier seven-message-product runs failed (timeouts); the later focused case passed as separately recorded below. Cluster, paging-pressure, TLS, power-loss and broader version/security acceptance remain pending. Management API, persistence, address settings. target/artemis-native-progress-final.log passed against the actual release JAR: snapshot the stopped isolated broker volume after one confirmed record, publish a later record, restore the older nonempty volume, prove node/queue IDs are unchanged, and reject the later receipt. Matching receipts resume; altered digests, malformed receipts and empty replacement queues are rejected. The empty replacement remains empty. target/ui-artemis-native-progress.log passed 17 DOM cases. Seven-product mixed recovery is being rerun separately after a previous run recorded source/HTTP timeouts during host sleep. These results do not prove cluster, TLS, paging pressure or power-loss behavior. Admin retry diagnostics and focused recovery reruns PULSAR ADMIN TIMEOUT means a client-side admin timeout; PULSAR ADMIN CONNECT RETRY means a failed connection. The SDK can wrap either in an exception whose default status is 500, without receiving an HTTP 500 response. Check broker access logs before diagnosing a server error. PULSAR ADMIN REQUEST FAILED preserves an ambiguous generic SDK failure without inventing an HTTP response. Actual HTTP response failures retain their status codes. Credential-provider/TLS rejections are permanent configuration faults; this classification does not constitute TLS interoperability acceptance. Snapshot preparation now emits deduplicated retry diagnostics with exception classes and stack locations, excluding exception messages, credentials, SQL and rows. A transient network fault retains RUNNING and the existing error generation; no manual resume should be needed. Inspect host/VM load, heap/direct memory, broker readiness, network and configured request timeouts rather than assuming a hardware-independent startup/catch-up deadline. After a full build, a focused fault rerun can reuse the accepted release and compiled tests: The checker refuses changed Java sources, stale tests/assets or an invalid release, and verifies the pinned Java-8-compatible JUnit console checksum. This runs one pipeline case , not the full 54-execution Maven suite. Default invocation still builds and runs the wider suite. Failed runs retain full Pulsar logs and bounded other-broker logs under target/broker-tests/ project / ; cleanup affects only that test project. Optional RIVOMESH TEST JAVA OPTIONS supplies JVM diagnostic flags to the isolated test and worker processes, for example -XX:+PrintGCDetails -XX:+PrintGCTimeStamps on Java 8. It is a test setting, not a production sizing recommendation. Latest focused acceptance target/messaging-pulsar-gc-diagnostics.log : one real pipeline case passed, zero failed/skipped , on the actual Java 8 release JAR (256 MiB worker heap). PostgreSQL plus Kafka/RabbitMQ/NATS/Redis/Pulsar/RocketMQ/Artemis complete snapshot/CDC, worker kill and three all-message-broker stop/start rounds; SQL continues during broker outage, retry diagnostics persist and clear automatically after catch-up. Finally deleting Artemis's initialized queue pauses only that target while all other subscriptions catch up. Native receipts restore through restart. This took about 590 seconds on the busy shared host, with Java 8 GC diagnostics enabled; no heap/deadline increase was used. It is one focused case, not a fresh pass of the entire 54-execution Maven suite, nor a general capacity/recovery-time promise.

title: Node registry
text: Shared node registry and heartbeat For current deployment, see the multi-node guide. Accounts, sessions and audit can now be shared by explicitly enabling shared access. Registry-only installations keep them local. Task operations are local by default. Optional fixed-owner global control is integrated; explicit controller/Agent separation has initial acceptance, while automatic relocation and the full HA matrix remain open. 中文：节点目录. Contract: CP-01. This feature shares node observations. Accounts, sessions and audit can be shared by explicitly enabling shared access; task/configuration operations are local by default. Optional fixed-owner global control is integrated; explicit controller/Agent separation has initial acceptance, while automatic relocation and additional failover profiles remain open. ADMIN opens Node registry . Standalone mode shows one node with an ID retained in private node-id . With a shared control database, all endpoints in the same clusterId read the same directory. VIEWER/OPERATOR retain existing task grants without global registry access. Cards show release SHA/version, real JVM/architecture/CPU/heap, configured task/running capacities, registration epoch, database observation time, heartbeat/expiry and task IDs/Worker state/observation time. HEALTHY means a valid heartbeat lease, not healthy data destinations. STALE means expiry; STOPPED means graceful deregistration committed. Query failure clears old healthy cards instead of presenting cached success. Task lists are observations, not global configuration/scheduling authority. Task pages/actions are local by default; optional fixed-owner routing is described in global control. Do not copy/start configurations elsewhere merely because a node is STALE. CDC/target leases still govern execution; registry leases cannot authorize Worker takeover. Shared access, global commands and explicit separated execution have distinct profiles; see global control and execution lifecycle for current acceptance. Linux and Docker Use independent local control, task and report directories and unique stable nodeIds. Sharing controller.json/audit H2 directories or a PVC is not a shared control protocol. See platform-cluster.yml. Initial native control-store profiles are PostgreSQL17 and MySQL8.4. H2 memory is for in-process protocol tests. For MySQL use com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver , a MySQL URL and a database namespace. Tables require InnoDB/utf8mb4 bin; incompatible existing tables are rejected. Configure TLS through driver parameters; production TLS is not disabled automatically. Startup needs schema/database and control-table creation permissions plus SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and bootstrap session-lock access. Existing tables are never cleared/dropped; incompatible formats refuse startup. A shared SQL instance is possible with a separate namespace and dedicated privileges. nodeId, username/password and optional advertiseUrl support a whole-value $ ENV NAME reference. advertiseUrl is observational only, with no user info/path/query/fragment. Connection/query timeouts are bounded; directory APIs omit database URLs, credentials, paths and raw business data. heartbeatMillis is100–30000ms. leaseMillis is1000–300000ms and at least three heartbeat intervals. maximumNodes is1–10000. Defaults are2s/15s/1000. Lease/capacity are consistent cluster settings without online editing. Capacity includes retained STALE/STOPPED records; historical-node administration remains future work. Each node publishes up to200task observations. Keyset pages default to20nodes and allow at most50. Helm and native Kubernetes Set the real URL and an existing username/password Secret in values-cluster.yaml. Install independent releases/PVCs: Each release stays a single-replica Recreate deployment with a stable release-name nodeId. Increasing one Deployment's replicas while sharing its PVC is invalid. Registry-only accounts/sessions remain local. Enable shared access for shared identity/session continuity; this does not provide controller HA. For manual YAML edit/apply node-a and node-b, including image/store/Secret references. Static parity is checked; live Kubernetes/CSI/upgrades/controller HA remain unaccepted. See session HTTPS configuration. Failure handling and FAQ - NODE ID IN USE: another live incarnation holds this ID. Stop the duplicate or use a unique stable ID. After confirmed power loss, wait for expiry without editing epochs. - NODE REGISTRATION FENCED: a replacement owns the registration. The old process cannot renew or deregister it. Correct deployment IDs and restart; this does not establish Worker takeover. - CONTROL STORE PROTOCOL MISMATCH: cluster format/lease/capacity differ or authority metadata is missing. Restore consistent settings/state; startup never overwrites it automatically. - CONTROL STORE UNAVAILABLE / readiness503: registry connection/query failure or expired heartbeat. healthz remains live; Workers follow their own journal leases. After recovery, an expired but unreplaced incarnation re-registers with a higher epoch; replaced processes remain fenced. - Killed nodes briefly remain HEALTHY: until expiry, death cannot be confirmed. Use heartbeat/expiry timestamps; the observation window is not failover authorization. - Old process overwrites replacement: active-ID and incarnation/epoch checks reject old heartbeats and shutdowns. - Graceful shutdown did not show STOPPED: kill, storage failure or lost commit confirmation falls back to STALE through expiry. - Backup/restore: back up the SQL control namespace and each node's existing accounts/audit/configuration/reports. Restoring the registry alone does not restore tasks or provide HA. Rollback of metadata/epochs requires review; external immutable backup anchors remain unfinished. Development preview uses http://127.0.0.1:18088 and http://localhost:18089 for two endpoints reading one registry. Different hostnames avoid same-name cookies overwriting across ports. Existing private preview credentials remain; sign in separately. Acceptance fixtures are removed; the development preview remains available.

title: OceanBase
text: OceanBase destination and FAQ 中文：OceanBase V3. Example: oceanbase-v3.yml. Current scope V3 configuration, CLI, fan-out workers and the bilingual wizard are implemented. Native OceanBase CE 4.3.5.6 ARM64/Java 8 transactions, cross-database rollback, ownership/epoch fences, snapshots/types and partial CDC passed. Full mixed restart/recovery acceptance has not passed; the adapter remains EXPERIMENTAL. See the evidence. This does not claim all versions, clusters or Oracle-mode support. product: OCEANBASE uses MySQL Connector/J 8.4.0 and jdbc:mysql:// , normally port 2881. Connect to a MySQL-mode user tenant , usually with rivomesh@business , rather than root@sys . Every new connection verifies OceanBase identity, mode and a non-system tenant, then forces ob read consistency=STRONG . A MySQL wire version is not the OceanBase product version. Oracle mode, seekdb and other compatible products are outside this verified profile. Start and recover Fill in source candidates, the user tenant and explicit database mappings, then supply MYSQL PASSWORD and OCEANBASE PASSWORD . Source GTID/ROW/FULL and privileges are documented in the V3 manual; UI steps are in the console manual. In another terminal use status config/oceanbase-v3.yml . After repairing a deterministic failure, resume the affected target in the UI, or use resume config/oceanbase-v3.yml oceanbase-business 7 with the same java -jar ... prefix. Replace 7 with the current errorGeneration from status; never guess it. Resume retries the original transaction. OceanBase is V3-only; select it in the wizard and provide a user-tenant identity. Extra destinations can select PostgreSQL or other products independently. Data, transactions and indexes Explicit mappings send each source database to a destination database in the same tenant. A configuration can fan out to OceanBase, PostgreSQL and other targets with independent acknowledgements and pauses. Rivomesh can create mapped databases/tables; it does not provision clusters, pools, tenants or users. Business changes and the sink checkpoint commit in one destination transaction, with a metadata row lock and epoch fencing. An uncertain commit is resolved by rereading the sink checkpoint. Capture progress never substitutes for apply progress. Independent destinations do not share a global atomic commit. Keyless tables gain rivomesh row id to retain duplicate multiplicity; business users must not edit it. UINT64 uses DECIMAL(20,0), decimals keep declared precision, JSON uses native JSON, binary uses LONGBLOB, and temporal values follow the relational-target mappings. Supported source generated expressions are evaluated by the existing source adapter and their values are copied into ordinary target columns. Procedures, triggers, foreign keys, partition layouts, physical index distribution and generated expressions are not automatically reproduced. Existing incompatible targets require an adoption plan. The default uniquePolicy: DOWNGRADE BUSINESS converts business UNIQUE indexes into ordinary indexes. Primary/actual identity keys must remain unique. Plain BTREE/simple GSI can use the current ordinary-index plan; global routing, global uniqueness and source partition semantics are not preserved. Expressions, prefixes, descending keys, fulltext and spatial methods require an explicit plan. PRESERVE can retain representable business uniqueness, subject to native DDL constraints; it does not reproduce arbitrary GSI semantics. Downgrading assumes exclusive synchronization writes, valid source constraints and complete ordered source transactions. It does not guarantee uniqueness under independent target writes. Existing UNIQUE constraints are never silently dropped. Before takeover, stop incremental writes, reconcile the data and restore required constraints. The complete automated takeover workflow remains pending. Deployment and privileges Use the same V3 task document with Linux, Docker, Helm or native Kubernetes deployment. Rivomesh manifests do not deploy OceanBase itself; database operations manage production clusters, OBProxy, tenant resources and isolation. The target account needs metadata access and appropriate mapped-database/table/index creation and business/metadata read/write privileges. A successful connection check does not prove all DDL/DML privileges. Supply passwords through environment references or protected configuration. LOCAL Journal supports same-host recovery. Cross-host worker takeover uses the already-supported external PostgreSQL/openGauss/MySQL journal. journal.product: OCEANBASE is rejected until that backend has its own acceptance. Controller HA and live Kubernetes/CSI acceptance remain separate work. Failures and FAQ - Tenant mismatch: verify the user suffix, OBProxy routing and tenant compatibility mode. System/Oracle tenants are rejected; mode is never changed automatically. - Outage/restart: recognized transient connection failures back off and reconnect, then catch up from destination progress. Other sinks continue until journal backpressure applies. OceanBase manages its own leader elections; multi-node/OBProxy failover needs separate acceptance. - SQL failure: only the affected subscription pauses. Repair permissions, types or constraints, then use the current errorGeneration in UI/CLI to replay the original transaction. Restart does not bypass the pause or skip events. - Deleted tables/metadata: an empty replacement is not silently created under an old checkpoint. Preserve evidence and plan a rebuild. A normal resume cannot repair deleted data or lost history. - Why STRONG reads: a recovery decision must observe committed checkpoint state. WEAK reads can return an older value; URL settings cannot override this profile's STRONG requirement. - Why a separate product from MYSQL: the wire protocol is similar, but vendor, tenant and consistency requirements differ. - Source DDL: initial auto-creation does not imply complete online DDL. Unsupported structural changes retain safe progress and require a conversion plan; do not edit GTIDs to bypass them. Full DDL, reconciliation/repair and migration workflows remain pending. - Existing targets: compatible empty tables can pass shape/ownership checks. A newly adopted nonempty table needs a provable baseline and adoption plan even if it looks identical. Rivomesh does not silently clear it or attach an unproved checkpoint. - Capacity: fixture CPU/memory/disk quotas are correctness-test settings, not hardware throughput standards. Benchmark row width, transaction size, indexes, fan-out, backlog windows and tenant resources. Hardware capacity reports remain pending. Official references - Official Docker fixture and resource settings - MySQL-mode transaction control - System variables Test-image startup diagnostics The official all-in-one image is a fixture, not a production deployment. The current fixture sets instance memory limit=5G/system memory=1G, user resource-unit memory size=2G/log disk size=2G, instance logs5G/data2G, and a container limit of 6G/6 CPUs. These are test settings, not production capacity recommendations or throughput standards. Unit memory is not exclusively business-tenant memory: an actual 2GiB unit probe showed roughly 1GiB for the user tenant after splitting with its metadata tenant. Other tenants, caches and host load affect recovery. A boot success! banner is insufficient; this image can print it even when OBD memory checks prevented observer startup. Check the actual observer process, user-tenant connection, container health and OBD logs together. Do not delete existing data or skip synchronization checkpoints to repair inadequate startup resources. Do not blindly use obd cluster start -f ; this version's -f means force-delete, not bypassing resource checks. Recovery acceptance still pending All four mixed runs retain their failures. The first15s administrative-DDL timeout followed successful outage catch-up, worker kill and PostgreSQL constraint isolation. With revised timeouts/catalog checks, the 5GiB instance/2GiB unit remained in user-tenant initialization beyond the recovery deadline; increasing CPU did not make the full case pass. A probe showed roughly 1GiB for the user tenant, which alone does not establish root cause. The6GiB instance/3GiB unit was rejected by OBD's available-memory precheck and never launched observer, despite a success banner. Checks were not bypassed, transactions were not skipped and checkpoints were not reset. These results do not establish complete automatic recovery or attribute every failure to Rivomesh or OceanBase; investigation and full acceptance remain required.

title: Performance & runtimes
text: Performance measurement and hardware reference 中文：性能测量. Hardware capacity must come from reproducible measurements of a stated workload. No rows/second or recovery-time promise applies independently of CPU, memory, storage latency, network, row width, transaction size, table count, target count, indexes, journal mode and competing workloads. Reproduce the first baseline Build the release before starting the benchmark. Do not rebuild that JAR during a run. Python 3, Docker Compose and the three fixture images are required. On macOS, prefix the Python command with caffeinate -i to prevent idle system sleep; lid closure, manual sleep and other suspension still invalidate timing. For a specified resource envelope: The CPU and database-memory limits apply to each database container; the CPU limit also applies to the worker. Default limits are one CPU and 1 GiB per container, with a 256 MiB Java worker heap and 256 MiB database buffers. They are limits, not reserved or dedicated host resources. Results identify actual image IDs, Docker VM CPU/RAM, container limits, database durability settings, JVM version, workload and release SHA-256. The local journal uses a host bind mount; database files use fixture volumes. Record their physical storage separately. Every run uses a random Compose project and copies the release to target/benchmarks/ run-id /app.jar . It creates only its own source/target, ports remain internal, and cleanup removes only that project's containers/volumes. The copied release, private fixture configuration, bounded logs and report.json remain for review. Failed runs produce status: FAILED ; they must not become capacity reference rows. Inspect containers.log for startup/runtime failures. What the measurements mean Field Meaning --- --- snapshotVisibilitySeconds Worker startup through visibility of all initially loaded target rows; includes JVM startup, discovery and automatic target creation snapshotRowsPerSecond Initial row count divided by that visibility interval sourceMutationSeconds Time to commit updates, deletes and inserts at the source cdcCatchUpSeconds First source mutation through visibility of the final target state; includes source writes cdcChangesPerSecond Number of changed rows, including deleted and inserted rows, divided by that interval afterWritesCatchUpSeconds Observed time between finishing source writes and observing the final target state snapshotContentSha256 , cdcContentSha256 Source and target ordered row streams must match, including IDs, versions and exact payload bytes Transactions are bounded to at most 500 changed rows. Validation streams row bytes rather than collecting the dataset in Python memory. Byte validation runs after each timed phase; a count-only match cannot produce a passing report. The final target contains updated rows, the expected deletes and newly inserted rows. Polling and Docker CLI overhead are included in observation times. This profile is one MySQL 8.4 source, one PostgreSQL 17.12 target, one primary-key table, fixed-width ASCII payload and a LOCAL journal. Source loading warms caches; it is not a cold-storage experiment. It measures neither peak sink throughput nor p95/p99 event latency, durable snapshot-END acknowledgement, failover RTO or steady-state saturation. It does not establish JSON/keyless/large-catalog, multi-target, external-journal, commercial database or cluster performance. Building the hardware standard Keep raw reports and run at least three repetitions for every workload/resource combination. Report medians and ranges; compare identical artifacts, versions, durability, dataset and storage. Record idle and loaded host conditions, disk latency/IOPS, network RTT/bandwidth, utilization and sustained backlog growth. Do not extrapolate linearly from CPU quotas or this small local profile. The final reference matrix still needs independent physical-host runs, remote targets, row-width/transaction/table-count sweeps, all targets and both journal modes, sustained soak, consumer backpressure, capacity exhaustion and recovery under backlog. An individual passing smoke run is evidence that this harness works for that dataset, not completion of that matrix. Recorded harness smoke acceptance Raw report: 1,000 initial rows / 256-byte payload, 1,200 CDC changes, both exact row-stream SHA-256 comparisons matched and isolated cleanup succeeded. Actual MySQL 8.4.13 / PostgreSQL 17.12 / Temurin 8u512; one CPU and 1 GiB per container, worker heap 256 MiB. Host Apple M1 Pro / 16 GiB; shared Docker VM and other workloads, start load average 66.59. Recorded startup-inclusive snapshot visibility 23.08 s and write-inclusive CDC catch-up 1.94 s. This verifies the harness, not a representative capacity result or a hardware standard. No repeated-run or saturation claim follows from it. Runtime and journal profiles --java 8 11 17 21 25 selects the corresponding Temurin JRE worker image; default is 8. --journal-mode LOCAL EXTERNAL defaults to LOCAL. The EXTERNAL profile uses a separate journal schema on the same PostgreSQL instance as the target, so journal and sink compete for that container's resources. It is not a remote dedicated journal benchmark. For example: Selecting a runtime is not a compatibility claim. Inspect a passing raw report and actual JVM version. This SQL profile can establish only MySQL-source/PostgreSQL-target snapshot/CDC coverage on that runtime; messaging/security/failover and other drivers need separate runtime acceptance. To run every listed JRE against both journals sequentially, using one unchanged release: The matrix retains progress and per-profile logs in target/runtime-matrix/ id /matrix.json , links each raw benchmark report, and continues independent profiles after a failed profile. A passing profile requires source/target byte checks, observed journal backend, successful cleanup, the expected actual JVM version and the same release SHA-256. Changing the release aborts the matrix. These remain small SQL runtime checks; they do not validate every adapter on every JRE. Do not run other integration suites or rebuild concurrently. Accepted SQL runtime matrix The ten-profile matrix passed on Temurin 8u512, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13 and 25.0.5, each with LOCAL and PostgreSQL EXTERNAL journals. Every run loaded 1,000 rows, applied 1,200 row changes and matched both full ordered byte-stream digests. Actual journal storage and JVM version were checked; every isolated cleanup succeeded. All used release SHA-256 2985bbbb51b84ec8de97d8a9b44c88d5a5a1d737032b1e13263d03d4a9134aa0 . The archive index identifies every unmodified raw profile report and its SHA-256; the raw matrix retains original workspace report paths. These are small runtime checks on a busy shared host, with no cross-JRE throughput comparison or all-adapter compatibility claim. The first cold JVM runs varied substantially, reinforcing why these results are not a hardware capacity standard.

title: Multi-database pipelines
text: Multi-database, multi-target pipelines This manual covers multi-database, multi-target synchronization. formatVersion: 3 (V3 in some console labels) identifies the task configuration format, not a database version or development phase. Keep the default for new tasks; changing the number does not migrate an existing task. 中文：多库、多目标运行手册. Updated 2026-11-15. Pipelines run through the CLI and Web console. The wizard defaults to the multi-database, multi-target format and retains the older single-database format. Formats/metadata are isolated; automatic migration of old state is not implemented. Web wizard and recovery After signing in, create a task: 1. Keep the default task format, enter the logical source, comma-separated databases, replication serverId and credentials. 2. Map each database explicitly. Add target instances with distinct IDs and their mappings. Select local or external transactional journals and quota. The plan masks every password, including JDBC URL passwords. Saving leaves the task stopped; check before starting. 3. Inspect snapshot/backlog and each subscriber's ACK. “Resume this target” uses its own error generation; global “Resume after repair” uses the pipeline generation. They are distinct operations. 4. Local stop only stops this worker. Shared pause blocks standby claims and attempts target-local fence confirmation. Unreachable targets remain unconfirmed, not falsely declared settled. Global resume does not clear independent target SQL pauses. Web local journals use the controller's private journals/ pipelineId directory. New YAML omits journal.path ; imports selecting an existing CLI journal path are rejected until a journal/target migration plan is prepared. Do not delete old state to bypass this check. External journals can be imported directly. Controller restart retains task/pause intent and the same managed journal/checkpoints. VIEWER/OPERATOR/ADMIN, local accounts/token rotation, exact task grants, configuration editing/history restore and durable audit are implemented. Managed row validation and planned repair have initial MySQL/PostgreSQL acceptance; see validation and repair. Manual patch/skip and automated cutover remain unfinished. DOM and real HTTP/database controls passed; visual and live Kubernetes UI acceptance remain pending. Configure and start Use pipeline-v3.yml. List databases within one logical MySQL topology in databases . Each target explicitly maps source databases to destination schemas/databases with mappings . Targets may subscribe to different subsets; every source database needs at least one target. Transactional products include GAUSS , POSTGRESQL , and MYSQL , plus first experimental KINGBASE, DM and OCEANBASE profiles within their documented acceptance boundaries; KAFKA / RABBITMQ / NATS JETSTREAM / REDIS STREAMS / PULSAR use the messaging protocol and map to message namespaces. Each target owns a delivery thread so stalled I/O cannot block others. MySQL journal/targets must be separate physical instances from the source: server uuid checks reject feedback loops even through address aliases. check reads source objects and target connections without initializing state or creating tables. It does not establish all DDL/snapshot privileges. Running creates metadata and missing business tables. Existing tables must match, be empty, and have no foreign keys/triggers. Nonempty targets require a migration plan and are blocked without clearing data. The synchronizer exclusively writes subscribed business tables. Sources require GTID, ROW/FULL, replica-update logging, no transaction compression/partial JSON images, and no anonymous/tagged GTIDs. Snapshots additionally need permission for short FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK : establish the InnoDB read view, verify schema, record GTIDs and open the cursor before releasing the lock. Reading a large table retains its MVCC view and metadata lock; monitor source undo history and waiting DDL. Snapshot, CDC and recovery The UI separates source snapshot preparation from destination delivery. TARGET SNAPSHOT remains active until every subscription has confirmed the current source manifests. “Source snapshot rows” counts source artifacts; each target has its own confirmed-table count. A message confirmation is still not consumer completion. Each completed target table is acknowledged immediately, allowing its source parts to be reclaimed once all targets confirm that table. Source commits and capture positions are journaled atomically. Each table has an independent snapshot baseline and checksummed parts. Completed artifacts are reusable; an incomplete source snapshot restarts the whole table because a lost MVCC read view cannot resume. Target part checkpoints resume committed parts without duplicates. Keyless tables preserve every duplicate occurrence using rivomesh row id ; source columns conflicting with this name are rejected. Complete before images match one occurrence. Identity mutations and normalized events commit once in source order, and every target reuses that result. Slow replay never mutates identities again. JSON comparison ignores object order/numeric scale while preserving SQL NULL versus JSON null. Stored generated values come from the log. Whitelisted deterministic virtual expressions use versioned expressions and historical logged inputs, never current source rows. Destination columns are ordinary materialized columns. Evaluation pins the snapshot SQL mode and UTC. Unlisted functions, missing base images, or historical schema mismatches stop progress. This does not promise arbitrary client-session SQL-mode query semantics. Plan native generated columns and application writes before takeover. Each transactional target commits data and its checkpoint together under an epoch fence. Targets acknowledge independently; one paused target does not stop others. An uncertain commit is resolved by checking the destination transaction ID/content hash before acknowledging the journal. Multiple targets are not one distributed atomic transaction. Table snapshots can have different baselines; cross-table takeover requires a common catch-up point. The MySQL+transactional-SQL common-cut Java service passed initial native acceptance; see Reconciliation foundation. Managed row comparison and planned repair are covered by the validation and repair manuals; business cutover remains pending. Retention follows the slowest subscriber, including paused ones. Snapshot parts are reclaimed only after every target confirms completion; manifests, baselines and keyless identities remain. Losing target metadata after artifact reclamation requires a rebuild plan. maxBytes covers logical event, normalized event, snapshot and identity payloads, including unconsumed normalization workspace reservations. Database indexes, WAL, metadata and free pages need additional capacity; reclamation does not immediately shrink physical files. Large-catalog pagination, physical headroom alerts, receipt compaction and oversized-transaction staging remain unfinished. Logical quotas are not total disk quotas. Raw capture reserves its normalization copy, keyless row IDs and potential identity additions. Normalization consumes that reservation atomically, preventing raw backlog from using the space needed to drain itself. When a slow destination exhausts available capacity, capture waits without advancing unpersisted GTIDs; deliveries, GC and lease heartbeats continue. Recovering consumers free space and capture resumes automatically. Local backpressure does not trigger the source-idle watchdog. Close/pause cancels the blocked receiver before waiting for the dump connection to finish. If one transaction and workspace exceed the entire quota, TRANSACTION EXCEEDS JOURNAL QUOTA preserves the old position. Insufficient snapshot/identity workspace, or old unreserved history that cannot be normalized after upgrade, raises JOURNAL WORKSPACE REQUIRES QUOTA PLAN . Source snapshots are currently all built before delivery; streaming reclamation across a large table, partial snapshot rebasing and oversized-transaction staging are unfinished. Expand capacity or use an explicit plan; never delete journal parts to make room. Quota is excluded from semantic identity: stop affected workers, change/reload configuration, then resume with the current global error generation. UI configuration editing remains pending. Journal choices LOCAL uses Java-8-compatible H2 2.2.224. path is a private directory, relative to the configuration file; it contains sensitive rows and receives mode 0700. Automatic server mode allows same-host CLI status/resume. It is not a cross-host database service. Preserve the whole directory/volume; do not copy a live .mv.db alone. Use EXTERNAL for cross-host takeover; shared-filesystem H2 has not been accepted as a cluster journal. EXTERNAL supports PostgreSQL, openGauss or a separate MySQL instance. Workers share journal instance/namespace/pipelineId and target configuration, with distinct nodeIds. Database-clock leases and epochs fence ownership. MySQL storage must use InnoDB and retain acknowledged commits across restart. External HA systems promote/fence database nodes; Rivomesh does not promote them. V3 worker-crash recovery, MySQL 8.4 async promotion and MGR election during snapshot passed; other versions/soak matrices still need acceptance. V2 results do not prove all V3 variants. Troubleshooting and FAQ - SQL errors: only that subscriber pauses with an error generation. Repair privileges/schema/data, then resume the original transaction using the current generation from status . Resume never skips data or edits GTIDs. - Connection loss/deadlocks: transient errors retry; local destination fencing blocks stale owners. Source reconnect validates candidate GTIDs and snapshot dependencies. Missing logs/multiple writers block or wait without rewinding progress. - Journal quota: CDC backlog uses the backpressure/recovery path above; snapshots or indivisible oversized commits need capacity/error-generation plans. Budget snapshot/identity copies, normalization reservation and the backlog window. Backpressure cannot reconstruct permanently lost storage or source binlogs purged before they were read. - Live DDL: currently blocks safely, including potentially unrelated-database SQL that could reference selected objects. Historical DDL evolution and explicit skip plans are unfinished. - UNIQUE(email): DOWNGRADE BUSINESS creates an ordinary secondary index. Source constraints, exclusive sync writes and transactional/idempotent checkpoints jointly preserve source uniqueness. Validate and restore constraints before application writes. Primary, identity and internal keys are never downgraded. - GSI: business GSI model entries can become ordinary indexes, losing global routing/uniqueness. Identity GSIs require a distribution plan. Existing GSIs/unique constraints are never blindly dropped. Commercial distributed GaussDB is not hardware-validated. - Expression/prefix/descending/special indexes: require a separate plan; the target pauses instead of silently omitting them. Unsupported indexes block before creating a missing table. - Types: common integers/unsigned, decimal/floating point, text/binary, YEAR, DATE/DATETIME/TIMESTAMP and JSON are covered. V3 now implements signed microsecond MySQL TIME durations with matching JDBC snapshot and TIME/TIME2 row-event text. Relational targets use INTERVAL/MySQL TIME(6); analytical/event targets retain duration text. See the Kingbase guide and DM guide for first native acceptance scope. BIT, ENUM/SET, spatial/zero dates, non-InnoDB and other objects need extension/testing. - V2 migration: continue the old configuration to retain v2 checkpoints. Adding formatVersion: 3 cannot take over a populated old target. Explicit data/state migration planning remains necessary. Replace 1 with the relevant subscriber or pipeline error generation. Stale requests are rejected. Permanent source errors persist as ERROR and block standby claims; pause reports each fence confirmation. RBAC/local accounts/configuration editing/audit are implemented. Managed validation/repair use the dedicated manuals and their limited acceptance profile. Manual patch/skip, cutover/failback and their Web workflows remain unfinished. LOCAL connection lifetime and controller memory The controller retains a stable connection to each opened LOCAL journal, including paused/stopped tasks, until configuration replacement or controller shutdown. On restart it opens existing files; inspecting a never-started task does not create its journal. Same-host CLI/certificate/repair operations therefore share a stable H2 automatic-server endpoint. Each opened journal has a 4 MiB page-cache setting plus schema/index metadata and connection-thread overhead. Worker heaps, control-store connections and IAM/audit state consume additional memory. Docker/Linux/Helm controller defaults now use a 512 MiB maximum heap; Helm exposes controllerHeapMiB . Size by initialized LOCAL journal count, schema volume and measured heap use; maxTasks limits task count. External transactional journals are available for larger installations.

title: Platform design
text: Rivomesh complete product and technical design Updated: 2026-11-15. 中文：完整方案. See requirements for decisions and status. This is the full design, not a claim that every feature is complete. V3 now supports multiple explicitly mapped databases within one logical MySQL source, fan-out, multiple configurations with isolated workers, optional durable journals and Web management. The v2 single-database/single-target mode remains compatible. See implementation status and validation for each adapter's accepted scope, and the console manual for operations. Remaining capabilities follow the phases below. 1. Product and scope Rivomesh serves enterprise/government database migration, continuous replication, data distribution, validation, and cutover orchestration. A bilingual Web workbench guides ordinary installations; configuration files, APIs, and CLI use the same model for experts. Dimension Scope --- --- Current delivery source MySQL, including existing 8.0/8.4 coverage; standalone, GTID replication, single-primary MGR Future sources PostgreSQL and Oracle; design Source SPI and neutral event/position models now, without claiming available connectors Relational targets MySQL, PostgreSQL, openGauss, distributed GaussDB, DM, Kingbase, OceanBase, GBase; profile product/version/mode/engine separately Analytics/warehouse targets ClickHouse, Apache Doris, Apache Hive; classify GBase analytical/transactional variants by actual capabilities Current delivery message targets Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ, RocketMQ, ActiveMQ (separate Classic/Artemis profiles), Redis Streams, NATS JetStream Deployment Linux manual, Docker, Kubernetes Helm, native Kubernetes manifests Storage Local durable journal, eligible target-hosted journal, independent shared journal Broad version coverage means an expanding compatibility matrix and capability detection, not unconditional support for every historical release/fork/combination. Mark features verified/experimental/unverified/unsupported and identify actual products, versions, modes, drivers, hardware, and recovery boundaries. JDBC connectivity is insufficient acceptance evidence. 2. Multiple tasks and targets Each independent configuration defines one logical source, object selection, multiple targets, mappings, storage, and resource policy. Different configurations may connect to independent MySQL clusters. Support standalone task processes and a console managing isolated workers. Never implicitly merge sources into one transaction or destination table. Tasks, subscriptions, tables, targets, configuration revisions, and stream generations have independent identities. Candidate endpoints belong to one topology; database mappings are explicit. Preflight detects overlapping destination writers, replication loops, changed source identity, and fingerprint conflicts. New targets establish their own baselines. Isolate rate, connection/thread, memory, and disk quotas per task. Independent configurations capture separately by default. Explicit capture sharing may follow after validating privileges, filters, retention, source identity, and recovery dependencies, not merely matching hosts. Preserve cross-database transaction atomicity only within a target scope supporting it; no cross-target global XA. 3. Modules and contracts - Source SPI: discover capabilities/objects, create consistent baselines, capture transactions/DDL, encode/restore positions, validate failover, acknowledge upstream. GTID is not a universal source abstraction. - Journal SPI: persist complete transactions/large-transaction fragments, publish atomically, checksum, recover, enforce quotas, and reclaim. Advance safe capture only after durable completion. - Sink SPI: capability/object planning, write/publish, resolve uncertain commits, idempotency/versioning, DDL recovery, visibility. Model transactional writes, versioned materialization, batch publication, and messaging explicitly rather than assuming JDBC transactions everywhere. - Control/Worker: leases/fencing, isolation, configuration revisions, resource scheduling, and recoverable operation logs. Console outages must not destroy deployed worker checkpoints. - Validation/Cutover: baselines/barriers, differences, restored constraints, write ownership, and audit. Event envelopes carry logical sourceId, streamGeneration, transaction identity/ordinal, schemaVersion, table identity, operation, before/after, field-presence bitmap, snapshot/DDL/transaction boundaries, source position, and origin. IDs remain stable across retries and physical source failover; new baselines/lineages use new generations. Timestamps are observational, not ordering authorities. Positions are versioned typed payloads: MySQL GTID/dependencies, PostgreSQL LSN/slot/database/instance lineage, Oracle SCN/transaction/redo context, interpreted by their adapters. Do not compare them lexically or retain only the maximum observed SCN/LSN while losing open long transactions. Snapshot fragments also require stable IDs, completeness markers, and checkpoints. Future PostgreSQL capture must handle exported snapshots, slot/WAL retention, REPLICA IDENTITY, unchanged TOAST fields, and failover-slot readiness. Oracle requires supplemental logging, redo/archive coverage, long transactions, RAC/CDB/PDB, LOBs, and lineage. Official references describe readiness requirements for PG slots and supplemental logging for Oracle CDC. PostgreSQL, Oracle CDC reference. Review driver/capture distribution terms separately; future connectors are not existing failback channels. 4. Target capabilities and consistency Target class Write design Boundary shown in UI --- --- --- MySQL/PG/domestic transactional databases Dialect-specific batches or native upsert; local apply checkpoint commits with business data Source-transaction atomicity within supported target scope; central control storage does not replace the local checkpoint ClickHouse Stable materialization identity, monotonic version, delete markers; engine-specific replacement/read views Background ReplacingMergeTree merges do not guarantee deduplicated raw reads; validated FINAL/view contracts, no assumed cross-table transaction Doris Validated Unique Key/Merge-on-Write, sequence, deletes, Stream Load batch protocol Detect actual single/multi-table commit scope; resolve labels/txn state, timeouts, and retention windows per version Hive ACID capability mode or immutable file/partition/snapshot publication Ordinary tables are not row-oriented replicas; profile update/delete, visibility, transactions, and compaction Messaging Publish change events and transaction/snapshot boundaries with stable IDs Publisher confirmation is not downstream business completion; at-least-once by default, consumers must be idempotent ClickHouse replacement uses ORDER BY; mutable attributes or unstable partitioning cannot define row identity. Keep routing stable and coordinate old-version/tombstone cleanup with the oldest replayable position. Official engine guide. Doris Unique Key is a row-materialization model, distinct from a relaxable source business secondary UNIQUE. Do not mechanically replace it with Duplicate Key. Resolve lost acknowledgments against actual commit state; expired labels are not permanent deduplication evidence. Sequence columns, load transactions. These references do not guarantee every older version. Hive publication records batches, file manifests/digests, partitions, schemas, and metadata commit state. Readers must not see temporary files; object storage cannot be assumed to provide atomic rename. Recovery reconciles files/catalog to prevent duplicates, partial batches, and orphans. ACID mode instead uses validated transaction APIs/configuration and compaction. Hive Transactions. Analytical targets default to data-service/warehouse output, not unverified OLTP application takeover destinations. Expose captured (durably collected), delivered (accepted), applied/materialized, visible under the declared read contract, and validated at a barrier as supported. A single success indicator must not hide these differences. 5. No-PK tables, JSON, generated columns All three are first-release requirements needing development; current code rejects them. Removing validation does not implement support. Identity class Planned strategy --- --- Primary key Stable keyed scan/lookup, including key changes No PK but a reliable all-NOT-NULL unique candidate Validate semantics, use it as identity, handle changes; do not casually relax this identity constraint No unique key; identical duplicate rows allowed Consistent baseline, multiset semantics, durable technical identities/counts, exact before-image matching; each change modifies one occurrence A target auto-ID, unique whole-row hash, or online OFFSET cursor cannot solve keyless identity. Hashes only accelerate candidates; compare full typed values and preserve multiplicity. Never delete every equal row for one logged deletion. Added technical columns require explicit mappings/views and dependency checks; they cannot be claimed invisible to SELECT . Keyless snapshotting needs a replayable consistent artifact coordinated with the log baseline. Persist fragments/manifests before loading and replaying later transactions; deduplicate imports by fragment/transaction identity. If a source MVCC snapshot disappears with its connection, a row number cannot restore it. Resume completed artifacts or rebuild that table at a provable new baseline without resetting unrelated completed subscriptions. The same applies to failover during an unfinished keyless snapshot. Explain required coordination privileges, possible short locks/rescans, and disk costs; do not promise arbitrary keyless tables lock-free exact row-cursor recovery. MySQL row-search behavior is a design reference, not reused storage internals. JSON: decode MySQL binary JSON correctly, preserving numeric precision, SQL NULL versus JSON null, array ordering, and characters. Map to native JSON or text/LOB with declared query differences. Compare using documented semantic normalization rather than object-key ordering/whitespace. Initially require full JSON logging and retain empty binlog row value options unless partial-patch/historical-base recovery is implemented. MySQL JSON replication. Generated columns: distinguish STORED/VIRTUAL, actual logged presence/values, dependencies, and schema versions. Choose proven equivalent target expressions or ordinary-column materialization. Missing logged values require evaluation from historical inputs, never a later SELECT of the source's current row. Translation/evaluation covers SQL mode, collation, time zones, precision, and JSON functions; unsupported expressions produce precise blockers/alternatives, never silent NULLs. Do not INSERT explicit values into native target generated columns. Record takeover differences between materialized ordinary columns and native generation. MySQL generated columns. 6. DDL, existing targets, constraints Discover/version table definitions, indexes, expressions, and dependencies. Ordered DDL needs schema barriers and recoverable operation logs. Classify transformations as automatic, planned migration, or blocked; never forward arbitrary source SQL. Reconcile catalogs after nontransactional DDL, restarts, and uncertain responses. Existing-target paths: compatible empty tables; nonempty staging/shadow comparison/publication; explicit merge policies using reliable keys; or incremental onboarding with proven matching data and log position. Entering a GTID without a verified baseline is insufficient. Keyless merges require multiset rules, not guessed upserts. Report extra/conflicting rows and trigger/FK side effects before changing anything; no automatic clearing. Relax Gauss business secondary UNIQUE to ordinary indexes; permit capability-driven relaxation for incompatible constraints on other targets, retaining original definitions. Preserve PK/candidate identity, internal deduplication, and required analytical materialization keys. Report missing equivalents instead of inventing indexes. See index policy for GSI and constraint restoration. 7. Three journal deployment modes Mode Use Availability/recovery limits --- --- --- LOCAL Single-host/Docker without extra services; persistent directory/PVC Process recovery; cross-node takeover requires original logs, authoritative owner verification, and old-writer fencing, otherwise automatic HA is disabled TARGET Reuse a validated transactional target's metadata schema No independent store, but its outage may block capture; not the default for ClickHouse/Hive/MQ-only tasks EXTERNAL Independent HA journal/state adapter and worker takeover Better isolation, but validate backend/acknowledgment/reclamation; arbitrary shared folders/object stores are not inherently safe journals Durable acknowledgment, checksums, transaction completion, stream sequence, and ownership form one protocol. Spill large transactions to durable fragments without marking partial transactions captured. Transactional sinks must not split an atomic source transaction just to save memory. Diagnose limits or use an explicitly supported mode rather than OOM and lose recovery context. Reclaim according to the slowest active subscription and baseline dependencies. Alert/backpressure near quotas and show retention headroom. Abandoning a target's history requires an explicit resnapshot plan. A message broker as sink and as internal journal are different roles; a sink connector does not automatically implement its journal backend. 8. Seven messaging families Target Adapter concerns --- --- Kafka Partitioning, durable acknowledgments, producer idempotence/transactions, transactional-ID fencing, schema/compression; restart/external-checkpoint recovery still required Pulsar Partition/routing, stable producer identity/sequence, persistent topics, deduplication windows/transactions RabbitMQ Durable queues/messages, publisher confirms, mandatory/returns, uncertain resend after reconnect, bindings RocketMQ Versioned normal/FIFO support, routing keys, acknowledgment/retry; transactional messages do not automatically couple source-log commits ActiveMQ Classic / Artemis Separate protocol/driver profiles, persistent messages, session/send acknowledgments, transactions/reconnect; Artemis features do not imply Classic parity Redis Streams XADD, persistence/replication, streams/groups and retention; generated stream IDs do not replace eventId NATS JetStream Durable streams, publish acknowledgment, subjects/consumers, deduplication IDs/windows, quotas; not ephemeral Core NATS The common contract is at-least-once publication with stable eventId and consumer idempotency by event ID/row version. Start with JSON envelopes and allow Avro/Protobuf/schema-registry plugins without a mandatory registry. Preserve type information and notify versioned schema/DDL changes. Choose per-table/key ordering or whole-transaction single-partition routing. Partitions, redelivery, and concurrent consumers do not imply global order. Large messages/transactions require transaction IDs, fragment ordinals, completion counts/markers, and checksums; atomic consumer application waits for complete assembly. Boundary records identify filtering scope so consumers do not wait for excluded rows. Kafka/Pulsar broker transactions, deduplication windows, or idempotent producers do not automatically provide end-to-end exactly-once across source, broker, and arbitrary consumer databases. RabbitMQ explicitly documents duplicates after lost confirmations. RabbitMQ reliability. Every adapter needs uncertain-commit recovery tests. Redis Streams and JetStream have their own retention, acknowledgment, persistence, and deduplication configurations; API availability is not durable-delivery validation. Redis Streams, JetStream. Validate ActiveMQ variants separately: Classic transactions, Artemis deduplication. Never skip bad messages by default. Missing routes, oversized messages, and serialization failures pause publication with guided UI repair. Any future quarantine-and-continue mode must retain replayable events and explicitly downgrade transaction/completeness guarantees. Broker retention/consumer completion are separate monitoring layers after publication; publish progress must not claim every subscriber has processed an event. 9. Fault model Cover source promotion/replication I/O and SQL errors, split writers, process/node failure, target outages/SQL errors, uncertain commits, disk full/corruption, interrupted DDL, lost MQ acknowledgments, duplicates/reordering, partial analytical batches, upgrades, and backup rollback. Retry transient errors with backoff; pause affected subscriptions for deterministic issues. Restarts/standby activation never bypass pause. UI exposes cause, scope, last safe positions, backlog, and recommended actions, then retries the original unit after repair. Do not offer casual position editing/transaction skipping. External database HA owns promotion/old-primary isolation; CDC cannot reconstruct permanently lost source data. 10. Graphical workbench Wizard: scenario → connections/tests → objects/privileges → compatibility/constraints/storage/sizing → explicit mapping → execution plan → run/diagnose → barrier validation → cutover/handover. Pages include overview, connections/drivers, tasks/subscriptions, object differences, journal/capacity, indexes/DDL, validation, incident center, cutover plans, deployment diagnostics, and audit. Explain causes/next steps in plain language; experts can expand SQLState/vendor codes and sanitized diagnostics. Stable codes have equivalent Chinese/English explanations. Pause/resume, retry, mapping/concurrency changes, object repair, table rebuild, validation, and cutover use authorized APIs with request IDs, expected configuration versions, idempotency, background-operation state, and audit. Browsers never edit metadata tables directly. Destructive plans show affected objects/recovery points without default data deletion. CLI/files use the same service contract for automation/offline operation. Separate viewer, operator, migration, and credential roles. Never put passwords in logs/plain exports. Provide offline help, diagnostic bundles, metrics/alerts; telemetry upload is not a runtime requirement. UI recovery does not replace database administrators repairing source replication. 11. Linux, Docker, Kubernetes Linux delivery includes distributions, configuration, start/status/stop/upgrade procedures, and systemd. Docker includes pinned images, health checks, durable mounts, and credential injection. Declare x86 64/ARM64, JDK/driver, and native dependencies only after validation; Java bytecode portability does not prove native-library portability. Deliver both Helm Chart (values/schema, templates, upgrades, persistence options) and native YAML (applicable ConfigMaps, Secret references, Services, workloads, probes, RBAC, PVCs), usable with kubectl apply. Maintain both through the same configuration model and render/consistency checks. Test defaults/local volumes/external storage/HA/upgrades; screenshots or hand-written-resource instructions are insufficient. Local authoritative journals require recoverable volumes and single-writer policy; shared-journal workers may have no authoritative local state. Replica count is not safe takeover, and RWO is not fencing. Validate/version configuration/Secret changes. Graceful stop completes or rolls back the current safe unit and releases ownership. Separate liveness, readiness, and subscription status to avoid restart storms during source outages or pauses. Support private registries, offline dependencies/driver packages, and certificates. Cryptographic, OS/CPU, and vendor certifications require actual dependency/testing records; do not claim certification by default. 12. Hardware/performance standard Deliver benchmark tools, workload definitions, raw reports, and sizing guidance rather than invented rows-per-core figures. 4C/8GiB, 8C/16GiB, and 16C/32GiB may be experimental tiers , not measured throughput or production minimums. Record source, worker, journal, and each target's hardware separately. Record CPU model/architecture/quota, RAM/heap, disk type/capacity/measured bandwidth/IOPS/durability settings, network RTT/bandwidth, product/driver versions, tables/indexes, row width, JSON/LOB, identity class, transaction sizes, operation mix, target count, batches/concurrency, and acknowledgment policy. Measure snapshot rows/s and MiB/s, CDC events/s and transactions/s, end-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency, visibility delay, backlog growth, takeover/catch-up time, resource use, source business impact, and final validation. Separate keyless, fan-out, MQ, JSON, and transaction-size cases. Narrow single-table benchmarks cannot represent all deployments. For backlog B, incoming rate r, and apply capacity c in matching units, sustained catch-up requires c r; ideal catch-up time is B/(c-r). Journal sizing approximates durable log rate × required retention plus active snapshot artifacts, large-transaction staging, index/metadata space, and margin, adjusted for measured compression/write amplification. More hardware cannot remove hot-key ordering, source/target bottlenecks, or network limits. 13. Migration, parallel service, extensions Scenario Boundary and extension --- --- Online migration/read-only mirrors Snapshot+CDC, data/object reconciliation, secondary-constraint conversion, migration reports Both environments serving reads One authoritative writer; route reads according to table/target watermarks and explicit staleness budget Gradual/domain cutover Explicit table/domain ownership, application routing, cross-domain transaction boundaries; service does not silently change application endpoints Independent writers to the same table Requires bidirectional capture, conflict rules, origin/loop prevention, key allocation, repair; two opposing tasks are insufficient Failback after cutover Before new business writes, planned routing rollback may suffice; afterwards require verified reverse capture/compensation and validation Real-time warehouse/events ClickHouse/Doris/Hive and all seven messaging families with traceable events/schemas Application compatibility SQL/object assessment, read-only shadow queries, interface regression, performance reports; data migration does not automatically port application SQL Cutover gates include freezing relevant source writes/DDL, final barriers, target apply/visibility, data validation, restored constraints/generated behavior, synchronization fencing, and application handover. Open new writes only after required gates pass; do not promise automatic application changes or unconditional zero downtime. Extensions include lineage/audit, history/CDC archiving, data-quality rules, masked distribution, rehearsals, and capacity forecasts. Transformations/masking mark outputs as transformed, not exact mirrors. PostgreSQL/Oracle capture should be later connector milestones before corresponding reverse paths can be validated.
